title: Κοιλία καὶ πόδες
part: The Belly and the Feet (Chambry 159 · Perry 130)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 159 (= Perry 130). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κοιλία καὶ πόδες περὶ δυνάμεως ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Koilia kai podes peri dynameōs ērizon.
sentences.l: The belly and the feet were quarrelling about power.
sentences.n: The two nouns stand without the article, as they do in the title — Greek names the parties of a fable bare, like the cast list of a play. ἐρίζω, 'to strive, wrangle', takes περί and the genitive of what is disputed; the imperfect ἤριζον keeps the quarrel running rather than settling it.

sentences.t: Παρ’ ἕκαστα δὲ τῶν ποδῶν λεγόντων ὅτι τοσοῦτον προέχουσι τῇ ἰσχύι ὡς καὶ αὐτὴν τὴν γαστέρα βαστάζειν, ἐκείνη ἀπεκρίνατο· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτοι, ἐὰν μὴ ἐγὼ τροφὴν ὑμῖν παράσχωμαι, οὐδὲ ὑμεῖς βαστάζειν δυνήσεσθε. »
sentences.tr: Par’ hekasta de tōn podōn legontōn hoti tosouton proechousi tēi ischyi hōs kai autēn tēn gastera bastazein, ekeinē apekrinato· « All’, ō houtoi, ean mē egō trophēn hymin paraschōmai, oude hymeis bastazein dynēsesthe. »
sentences.l: And the feet saying at every turn that they so far excel in strength as to carry even the belly itself, she answered: « But, you there, if I do not furnish you with food, neither will you be able to carry. »
sentences.i: And when the feet kept saying at every turn that they so far surpassed in strength as to carry even the belly itself, she answered: « But you there — if I furnish you no food, you will not be able to carry anything either. »
sentences.n: τῶν ποδῶν λεγόντων is a genitive absolute: the feet are not the subject of the main verb, which is the belly's. παρ’ ἕκαστα is 'at every point, at every turn'. τοσοῦτον … ὡς with the infinitive is the result construction, 'so far … as to'. ἐκείνη is feminine because κοιλία is, so the belly answers as 'she'; γαστήρ in the feet's own words is the same organ under another name. ὦ οὗτοι is a blunt way of hailing people, nearer 'you there' than 'gentlemen'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν στρατευμάτων τὸ μηδὲν ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ πλῆθος, ἐὰν μὴ οἱ στρατηγοὶ ἄριστα φρονῶσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai epi tōn strateumatōn to mēden epi to poly plēthos, ean mē hoi stratēgoi arista phronōsin.
sentences.l: So too in the case of armies the great multitude is nothing, if the generals are not of the best judgement.
sentences.i: So too with armies: for all their numbers they count for nothing, unless the generals have the best judgement.
sentences.n: Οὕτω καί, 'so too', maps the story onto life. The Greek is compressed to the point of strain: no copula is written, and ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ πλῆθος follows ἐπὶ τῶν στρατευμάτων in a different case, so the sense has to be gathered as 'the great host amounts to nothing'. The reading is Chambry's page as it stands, and the strain is his text's, not a slip in transcription. ἄριστα φρονεῖν is to be of the best judgement — φρονεῖν is having one's wits about one, not thinking a particular thought.
